items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A person who has fled their country owing to a well-founded fear of persecution and is protected under the 1951 Refugee Convention"?
items.answer: refugee
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of refugee.

items.stem: Distinguish between emigration and immigration.
items.answer: Emigration is leaving a country to live elsewhere; immigration is arriving in a new country to live.
items.markingKey: Emigration is leaving a country to live elsewhere; immigration is arriving in a new country to live. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Leila writes: "Migration is mainly a modern phenomenon." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Humans have migrated throughout history, from early human dispersal out of Africa to the migrations of the 19th century.
items.markingKey: Humans have migrated throughout history, from early human dispersal out of Africa to the migrations of the 19th century. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source A – UNHCR report (paraphrased): Paraphrase of UNHCR, Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2023, Geneva, 2024

The report stated that the number of forcibly displaced people had risen for twelve consecutive years, driven by conflicts in Sudan, Myanmar, Ukraine and elsewhere. It noted that low- and middle-income countries hosted around 70% of refugees.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about types of migration: voluntary and forced, internal and international. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of UNHCR, Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2023, Geneva, 2024. Purpose: to inform governments and the public about displacement and appeal for support. Value: It is the main global source of displacement data, compiled from national and field data. Limitation: Numbers of IDPs are estimates in conflict zones and the agency also seeks funding, which may shape its emphasis.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of UNHCR, Global Trends: Forced Displacement in 2023, Geneva, 2024. Purpose: to inform governments and the public about displacement and appeal for support. Limitation: Numbers of IDPs are estimates in conflict zones and the agency also seeks funding, which may shape its emphasis. items.answer: Forced displacement keeps rising and is hosted mostly by poorer countries.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining migration."
items.answer: Both matter: push factors explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; their balance differs between forced and voluntary migration.
items.markingKey: From the source: Forced displacement keeps rising and is hosted mostly by poorer countries. Own knowledge for: conflict and disaster force people to leave regardless of destination; poverty and lack of jobs drive much rural–urban migration. Own knowledge against: migrants usually choose destinations with jobs, family networks and safety; many migrants are relatively better off and move for opportunities. Judgement: Both matter: push factors explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; their balance differs between forced and voluntary migration. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. items.stem: According to UNHCR, about how many people were forcibly displaced worldwide by mid-2024?
items.answer: About 120 million
items.markingKey: B. This includes refugees, asylum seekers and IDPs.

items.stem: Explain why internally displaced people may be more vulnerable than refugees.
items.answer: IDPs remain under their own government, which may be causing or unable to stop the conflict, and they lack the international legal protection of refugee status.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: IDPs remain under their own government, which may be causing or unable to stop the conflict, and they lack the international legal protection of refugee status. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Use Census of India migration tables, two research papers and interview transcripts; categorise factors; map flows; evaluate sources; cite in APA.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Middle Passage"?
options: The trade route linking Europe (manufactured goods), West Africa (enslaved people) and the Americas (sugar, cotton, tobacco)
The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, created in 1950 to protect and assist refugees
The sea voyage across the Atlantic in which enslaved Africans were transported in brutal conditions
A reason that attracts people to a place, such as jobs, safety or better services
items.answer: The sea voyage across the Atlantic in which enslaved Africans were transported in brutal conditions
items.markingKey: C. "Middle Passage" is the sea voyage across the Atlantic in which enslaved Africans were transported in brutal conditions.

items.stem: Distinguish between the abolition of slavery and the abolition of the slave trade.
items.answer: Abolishing the trade (Britain 1807) banned buying and transporting enslaved people; abolishing slavery (Britain 1833) freed people already enslaved.
items.markingKey: Abolishing the trade (Britain 1807) banned buying and transporting enslaved people; abolishing slavery (Britain 1833) freed people already enslaved. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Enslaved Africans did not resist slavery." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Resistance included revolts (such as the Haitian Revolution from 1791), escape, sabotage and preserving culture.
items.markingKey: Resistance included revolts (such as the Haitian Revolution from 1791), escape, sabotage and preserving culture. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

The historian argued that the indenture system recreated many features of slavery: recruitment by fraud, crowded voyages, harsh plantation discipline and criminal penalties for absence from work. He concluded that it was "a new system of slavery".

items.answer: Indenture reproduced many abuses of slavery.

items.stem: How many years passed between Britain abolishes the slave trade (1807 CE) and Indian indentured emigration is stopped (1917 CE)?
items.answer: 110 years
items.markingKey: 110 by subtraction (M1 A1). BCE years count down towards 1 BCE; the year after 1 BCE is 1 CE.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Indentured labour was simply slavery under another name."
items.answer: Thesis: Indenture was not identical to slavery, because workers were not owned for life, but its coercion and abuses justify the description of a "new system of slavery".
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many labourers were deceived and faced brutal conditions and penalties; the system served the same plantation economies. Counter-arguments: labourers had contracts, wages and a fixed term, and many chose to stay as free settlers; the system was eventually reformed and abolished after protest. Thesis/conclusion: Indenture was not identical to slavery, because workers were not owned for life, but its coercion and abuses justify the description of a "new system of slavery". Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Explain why European colonial powers turned to indentured labour after the abolition of slavery.
items.answer: Plantation owners in places such as Mauritius, Trinidad, Guyana and Fiji still needed cheap labour for sugar, so they recruited workers from India and China on fixed contracts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plantation owners in places such as Mauritius, Trinidad, Guyana and Fiji still needed cheap labour for sugar, so they recruited workers from India and China on fixed contracts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between enslavement and indentured labour.
items.answer: Enslaved people were owned as property for life with no rights, and their children were enslaved too; indentured labourers signed (often unfair) contracts for a fixed term and were legally free afterwards.
items.markingKey: Enslaved people were owned as property for life with no rights, and their children were enslaved too; indentured labourers signed (often unfair) contracts for a fixed term and were legally free afterwards. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe the Haitian Revolution and explain what it reveals about resistance to slavery.
items.answer: Beginning in 1791, enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up under leaders including Toussaint Louverture; Haiti declared independence in 1804. Enslaved people overthrew slavery and created the first independent Black republic.
items.markingKey: Context (Beginning in 1791, enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose up under leaders including Toussaint Louverture; Haiti declared independence in 1804.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: enslaved people overthrew slavery and created the first independent Black republic. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to resistance to slavery.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rehabilitation"?
options: The movement of people from one place to another to live, either permanently or for a long period
Money sent home by migrants to their families
Helping displaced people rebuild their lives through housing, land, jobs and compensation
Migration that people are compelled to undertake because of conflict, persecution, disaster or development projects
items.answer: Helping displaced people rebuild their lives through housing, land, jobs and compensation
items.markingKey: C. "rehabilitation" is helping displaced people rebuild their lives through housing, land, jobs and compensation.

items.stem: Distinguish between refugees in 1947 and internally displaced people today.
items.answer: Many 1947 migrants crossed the new international border and became citizens of the new state; IDPs today remain displaced within their own country without crossing a border.
items.markingKey: Many 1947 migrants crossed the new international border and became citizens of the new state; IDPs today remain displaced within their own country without crossing a border. items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why refugee resettlement was a major challenge for India and Pakistan after 1947.
items.answer: Millions arrived with few possessions, needing housing, land, jobs and compensation; both new states had limited resources and had to build camps and new towns, such as colonies in Delhi. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.answer: The new border divided mixed communities; many people feared becoming minorities in the new state, and violence and insecurity drove Hindus and Sikhs to India and Muslims to Pakistan.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "integration"?
options: The process by which migrants become part of the host society while keeping aspects of their own culture
The boundary between India and Pakistan drawn by Cyril Radcliffe and announced on 17 August 1947
Migration chosen freely, for example for work, study or family
The trade route linking Europe (manufactured goods), West Africa (enslaved people) and the Americas (sugar, cotton, tobacco)
items.answer: The process by which migrants become part of the host society while keeping aspects of their own culture
items.markingKey: A. "integration" is the process by which migrants become part of the host society while keeping aspects of their own culture.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why migration can create tensions in host communities.

items.stem: Remittances received by India was 53.5 US$ billion in 2010 and 120 US$ billion in 2023 (World Bank). Calculate the percentage change.

items.answer: Thesis: For many countries the benefits of remittances outweigh the costs, but the loss of skilled workers can be serious, especially in health care in small, poor countries.

items.stem: The number of forcibly displaced people worldwide went from 42.7 million in 2012 to 117.3 million in 2023. Which is the percentage change?

Source A – Oral history (paraphrased): Paraphrase of an interview recorded by the 1947 Partition Archive, 2015

The interviewee, a schoolgirl in Lahore in 1947, recalled that her family left in a hurry, taking only a few belongings and expecting to return in a few weeks. She described the long journey to Amritsar and the years spent rebuilding their lives in Delhi, and said she never saw her childhood home again.

Identify two points that Source A makes about Partition and refugee movements in the 20th century, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Families fled suddenly, expecting to return, and had to rebuild their lives.
items.markingKey: Families fled suddenly, expecting to return, and had to rebuild their lives. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem:

The brief reported that remittances to low- and middle-income countries reached about US$ 656 billion in 2023, more than foreign direct investment and official development assistance combined. India received the largest amount, followed by Mexico, China and the Philippines.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about the impacts of migration on source and host communities. Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of World Bank / KNOMAD, Migration and Development Brief 40, June 2024. Purpose: to inform policymakers about remittance trends. Value: It is a reputable international source using central bank data. Limitation: Official figures exclude informal transfers, so true remittances may be higher; it gives little detail on social impacts.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Indentured labour was simply slavery under another name."
items.answer: Indenture was not identical to slavery, because workers were not owned for life, but its coercion and abuses justify the description of a "new system of slavery".
items.markingKey: Arguments for: many labourers were deceived and faced brutal conditions and penalties; the system served the same plantation economies. Arguments against: labourers had contracts, wages and a fixed term, and many chose to stay as free settlers; the system was eventually reformed and abolished after protest. Supported judgement: Indenture was not identical to slavery, because workers were not owned for life, but its coercion and abuses justify the description of a "new system of slavery".

items.stem: Tariq is investigating types of migration: voluntary and forced, internal and international and proposes the research question: "Why do people move?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad and has no place or time Improved: "What push and pull factors explain migration from rural Bihar to Mumbai since 2000?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad and has no place or time); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "What push and pull factors explain migration from rural Bihar to Mumbai since 2000?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "The British government was mainly responsible for the suffering caused by Partition."
items.answer: Britain's rushed withdrawal bears significant responsibility, but the suffering also resulted from political decisions by Indian leaders and local violence; responsibility was shared.
items.markingKey: From the source: Families fled suddenly, expecting to return, and had to rebuild their lives. Own knowledge for: the hurried withdrawal and late announcement of the border left little planning or security; colonial policies had deepened communal divisions. Own knowledge against: Indian political leaders also agreed to Partition and could not control local violence; local communal tensions and armed groups drove much of the violence. Judgement: Britain's rushed withdrawal bears significant responsibility, but the suffering also resulted from political decisions by Indian leaders and local violence; responsibility was shared. items.stem: "Migration brings more benefits than costs to source countries." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For many countries the benefits of remittances outweigh the costs, but the loss of skilled workers can be serious, especially in health care in small, poor countries.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: remittances reduce poverty and provide foreign exchange; diaspora networks bring investment and ideas. Arguments against: brain drain weakens health and education systems; families are separated and economies can become dependent on remittances. Supported judgement: For many countries the benefits of remittances outweigh the costs, but the loss of skilled workers can be serious, especially in health care in small, poor countries. items.answer: girmitiya

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "voluntary migration"?
options: A person who has fled their country owing to a well-founded fear of persecution and is protected under the 1951 Refugee Convention
A reason that encourages people to leave a place, such as unemployment or conflict
A reason that attracts people to a place, such as jobs, safety or better services
Migration chosen freely, for example for work, study or family
items.answer: Migration chosen freely, for example for work, study or family
items.markingKey: D. "voluntary migration" is migration chosen freely, for example for work, study or family.

items.stem: Which 1948 conflict created a major Palestinian refugee population?
items.answer: The 1948 Arab–Israeli War
items.markingKey: D. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled; UNRWA was set up in 1949 to assist them.

items.stem: Diego writes: "Migrants are a burden on public services." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Studies in many countries show that working-age migrants often pay more in taxes than they use in services, though impacts vary.
items.markingKey: Studies in many countries show that working-age migrants often pay more in taxes than they use in services, though impacts vary. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between enslavement and indentured labour.
items.answer: Enslaved people were owned as property for life with no rights, and their children were enslaved too; indentured labourers signed (often unfair) contracts for a fixed term and were legally free afterwards.
items.markingKey: Enslaved people were owned as property for life with no rights, and their children were enslaved too; indentured labourers signed (often unfair) contracts for a fixed term and were legally free afterwards. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between an economic migrant and a refugee.
items.answer: A refugee flees persecution or conflict and is protected by international law; an economic migrant moves mainly to improve their income or opportunities.
items.markingKey: A refugee flees persecution or conflict and is protected by international law; an economic migrant moves mainly to improve their income or opportunities. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between internally displaced people today and refugees in 1947.
items.answer: Many 1947 migrants crossed the new international border and became citizens of the new state; IDPs today remain displaced within their own country without crossing a border.
items.markingKey: Many 1947 migrants crossed the new international border and became citizens of the new state; IDPs today remain displaced within their own country without crossing a border. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between impacts on the source country and impacts on the host country.
items.answer: Source countries gain remittances but may lose workers and skills; host countries gain workers and cultural diversity but may face pressure on services and social tensions.
items.markingKey: Source countries gain remittances but may lose workers and skills; host countries gain workers and cultural diversity but may face pressure on services and social tensions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between the abolition of the slave trade and the abolition of slavery.
items.answer: Abolishing the trade (Britain 1807) banned buying and transporting enslaved people; abolishing slavery (Britain 1833) freed people already enslaved.
items.markingKey: Abolishing the trade (Britain 1807) banned buying and transporting enslaved people; abolishing slavery (Britain 1833) freed people already enslaved. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

The historian argued that the indenture system recreated many features of slavery: recruitment by fraud, crowded voyages, harsh plantation discipline and criminal penalties for absence from work. He concluded that it was "a new system of slavery".

Limitation: It relies largely on official records and may give less weight to labourers' own voices and agency.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining migration." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Both matter: push factors explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; their balance differs between forced and voluntary migration.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: conflict and disaster force people to leave regardless of destination; poverty and lack of jobs drive much rural–urban migration. Counter-arguments: migrants usually choose destinations with jobs, family networks and safety; many migrants are relatively better off and move for opportunities. Thesis/conclusion: Both matter: push factors explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; their balance differs between forced and voluntary migration. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).
